title: Leadership The Two Kinds of Failure Mini Philosophy (Jonny Thomson)
author: Mini Philosophy
summary: Big Think's Jonny Thomson examines the philosophy of failure, distinguishing constructive failure — where we learn and grow — from destructive failure, which crushes self-worth or steers toward vice. Philosophers and psychologists identify two key domains for making failure constructive: the learner and the environment. For the learner, three practices foster openness: reframing ('I can't do this yet' vs. 'I can't do this'), separating the deed from the doer, and getting curious about what went wrong. But one's capacity for openness also depends on how much of oneself is invested in the outcome — we cannot will ourselves to a different starting point given personality and history, but we can choose how to go on. For the environment, the single biggest factor is other people: warm support from someone who wants us to win produces growth; hostile questioning produces defensiveness. The paradox: the more willing you are to accept failure, the more likely you are to succeed. Closing principle: fail, fail often, fail forward, fail among friends, and never let a stumble stop you from walking.
points: Constructive failure allows learning and growth; destructive failure crushes self-worth or reinforces learned helplessness — the same setback can be either depending on learner and environment.
The paradox of failure acceptance: the more willing you are to accept failure, the more likely you are to succeed.
Three learner practices: reframe ('can't do this yet'), separate the deed from the doer, and get curious — 'That's weird, why did that happen?' is far more useful than 'How dare you!'
We cannot will ourselves to a different starting point with personality or past, but we choose how to go on — habits of openness can be built incrementally.
Environment is the single biggest factor in learning from setbacks: we need people who support us and want us to win, not a Patrick who asks hostile questions for his own ego.
quotes: while failure is important and a life without failure is both impossible and undesirable, we should not then fetishize failure
The more willing you are to accept failure, the more likely you are to succeed. And it's something that comes far more naturally to the American mindset.

There's a valuable difference between 'I can't do this' and 'I can't do this yet.' Second, separate the deed from the doer. 'That was a bad shot' is about the single moment or action, but 'I'm rubbish at this' makes it about your talent.

If we are to be open about things, we should appreciate that our worth or even future happiness does not (usually) depend on this single failure. This is certainly true of bonsais and exam results, but it can even be true of a divorce or losing a job. We are not the things we do or the roles we play.
In my experience, the single biggest factor in determining whether I will learn from a setback or get riled up and angry is other people.
Fail. Fail often, fail forward, fail among friends. Never let a stumble stop you from walking.
